title: Measurement-enabled online quantum processing with amplitude encoding
authors: Giacomo Franceschetto, Pere Mujal, Rodrigo Martínez-Peña
abstract: We introduce a quantum reservoir computing online protocol that realizes amplitude encoding on quantum hardware. Our scheme combines mid-circuit measurement and reset operations to implement the partial-trace dynamics underlying amplitude encoding, while an indirect measurement scheme provides access to reservoir observables without interrupting temporal processing. In contrast to other approaches, our method preserves online operation, avoids input buffering, and keeps the runtime linear in the number of time steps. We present the theoretical formulation of the protocol and a proof-of-principle implementation on quantum hardware, and we evaluate its performance on two standard benchmark tasks. Our results show that the reservoir dynamics can be monitored through both direct measurements of the input qubits and indirect measurements of the memory qubits, enabling observation of the full system while isolating the internal evolution of the reservoir. This work provides a practical route toward scalable hardware implementations of amplitude-encoded quantum reservoir computing and opens the door to systematic experimental studies of complex quantum reservoirs.
summary: This paper presents a novel protocol for performing amplitude-encoded quantum reservoir computing online using mid-circuit measurements. By introducing an indirect measurement scheme, the authors overcome limitations of previous methods that required input buffering or complex resets. The work provides both theoretical foundations and hardware demonstrations showing scalable monitoring of complex quantum reservoir dynamics.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an online quantum reservoir computing (QRC) protocol that realizes amplitude encoding on physical quantum hardware while maintaining linear runtime scaling.
main_result: The proposed method successfully enables the monitoring of full system dynamics by combining mid-circuit measurements with a novel indirect measurement scheme, providing a practical path for scalable QRC implementation.
method: The core technique involves using mid-circuit measurement and reset operations to simulate partial trace dynamics required for amplitude encoding, supplemented by an ancillary qubit based indirect measurement protocol.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a quantum reservoir computing setup, comparing theoretical spin models (Ising Hamiltonian) with circuit implementations on hardware platforms like superconducting qubits or trapped ions concepts. The memory evolution follows recurrent dynamics $ho_u^k = L_k[ho_u^{k-1}]$.
key_observables: Expected values of Pauli operators ($\langle\hat{\sigma}_xangle, \langle\hat{\sigma}_yangle, \langle\hat{\sigma}_zangle$) for both input (direct) and memory (indirect) qubits; the capacity $C(\eta)$ of the reservoir.
important_parameters: Measurement strength parameter $\alpha$ (or related coupling constants like $g$), which controls the measurement backaction, ranging from projective ($\alpha=1$) to weak limits.
main_assumptions: Previous methods requiring input buffering or 'rewinding' are avoided; hardware limitations force approximations like nearest-neighbor Hamiltonians and finite time windows for long sequences.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the QRC circuit structure, compare dynamics across spin model/circuit simulation/hardware realizations, and plot capacity $C(\eta)$ versus measurement strength or observable combinations for forecasting tasks.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the theoretical protocol combining amplitude encoding via mid-circuit measurements with an indirect measurement scheme. It then details the mathematical formulation using both spin models and circuit maps before presenting proof-of-principle implementations and benchmarking on time series forecasting and STM tasks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the challenge of implementing complex, continuous quantum information processing protocols (like QRC) on noisy, discrete hardware by developing measurement techniques that preserve online operation and system observability.
